# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.

The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
of it.

## What to do

Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
providers.

Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.

A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
there is no opt-out flag.

Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
      count is `0`
- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
      exactly once
- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
      **not** contain the offending value
- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
      that the thrown message names the tool
- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
      round
- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
      pinned by a test
- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
      containing that field's value
- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
      `devDependencies`, and
      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
      merely present
- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
      returned to the model rather than thrown
- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
      properties pass through unmodified
- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
      bump is MINOR
- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface

## Tech notes

Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.

Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
authorization model); retry, timeout
and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
written against this contract later.

| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |

When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.

## Validation at execute time

- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16)).
- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46)).
- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults.
- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake.

## Schema compilation and caching

- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L94), [validated by: throws at registration time naming the tool for an uncompilable schema](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L4)).
- A static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call without re-reading or re-compiling `definition.inputSchema`.
- A function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` resolves its definition on each `execute` call and validates against the `inputSchema` returned for that call, caching compiled validators by schema object reference (`WeakMap`) so distinct returned schemas each enforce their own rules.

## Orchestrator tool-loop recovery

- Because a schema rejection returns a `ToolResponse` instead of throwing, `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` sends the rejection `result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` message, allowing the model to issue a corrected tool call on the next round and complete the turn within `maxToolRounds` ([validated by: returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L112)).

22	## Workflow Commands

24	### Development

26	npm run dev          # Start example/server.ts with hot reload (tsx watch)
27	npm run typecheck    # Run TypeScript type checking without emitting
28	```
29	
30	### Building
31	```bash
32	npm run build        # Compile TypeScript to dist/ (tsc)
33	npm start            # Run compiled JavaScript from dist/index.js
34	```
35	
36	### Testing
37	```bash
38	npm test             # Run Jest test suite
39	# Tests use ts-jest for TypeScript compilation
40	# Configuration: jest.config.js
41	```
42	
43	### Code Quality
44	```bash
45	npm run eslint       # Run ESLint with max-warnings 0 (zero-tolerance)
46	npm run prettier     # Format all src/**/*.ts with Prettier
47	npm run prettier:check  # Check formatting without writing
48	```
49	
50	### All Checks (Recommended Pre-Commit)
51	```bash
52	npm run verify
53	```
54	
55	That is the blocking set `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `verify` job runs on every
56	pull request, in the same order, and `scripts/verify-script.test.ts` fails if the
57	two stop agreeing - so this command cannot quietly become a subset of what CI
58	demands. Two gates in that job are missing from it because both diff against
59	`origin/main` and neither runs the same way on a checkout: the spec anchor check
60	and the changelog check.
61	
62	Two further CI jobs are worth running locally before a release or a change that
63	touches packaging: `npm run check:build-chain` (audit and action pins) and
64	`npm run smoke` (packs the tarball and installs it outside this tree).
65	
66	## Spec Header Table
67	
68	Every `specs/*/spec.md` opens with its title, then a two-column header table,
69	and carries a lead paragraph of prose before its first `##` section:
70	
71	```markdown
72	# <spec title>
73	
74	| Field  | Value                  |
75	| ------ | ---------------------- |
76	| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#<n> |
77	| Status | Draft                  |
78	
79	<lead paragraph>
80	```
81	
82	The lead paragraph does not have to sit immediately after the table: a spec
83	carrying a metadata block of its own may place that block between the two. What
84	the convention requires is that prose, rather than a section heading, follows
85	the header material, and that the prose runs to at least 40 characters -
86	anything shorter is reported as no lead paragraph at all.
87	
88	`Issue` names the issue the spec was written against, or `n/a` for the specs
89	that predate this convention.
90	
91	`Status` is one of `Draft`, `In Progress` or `Shipped`. It is not a mood, and
92	it is not a claim about how finished the feature is: it is the spec's own
93	test-citation coverage. No testable statement cited is `Draft`, some cited is
94	`In Progress`, all cited is `Shipped`. A spec describing shipped, working
95	behaviour still reads `Draft` until its statements cite the tests that
96	validate them.
97	
98	A spec that should no longer be graded takes a terminal value instead. The
99	parser buckets roughly sixteen labels into five buckets, and the two terminal
100	ones skip the coverage check whatever the citation count:
101	
102	| Written into the spec                                            | Bucket                       |
103	| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
104	| `Draft`                                                          | `draft`                      |
105	| `In Progress`, `In Review`, `Planning`, `WIP`, `Proposed`        | `in-progress`                |
106	| `Shipped`, `Implemented`, `Complete`, `Accepted`, `Done`, `Live` | `shipped`                    |
107	| `Retired`, `Superseded`, `Removed`, `Deprecated`, `Obsolete`     | `retired` - skips the check  |
108	| `Rejected`, `Abandoned`                                          | `rejected` - skips the check |
109	
110	Prefer the canonical `Draft` / `In Progress` / `Shipped` for a live spec; reach
111	for `Retired` or `Rejected` rather than leaving a superseded spec to claim a
112	coverage tier it will never earn.
113	
114	ADRs do not carry this table. They declare their state as YAML frontmatter
115	`status:` instead - `accepted` for a decision the code implements, `proposed`
116	for one it does not. That field does mean maturity, which the spec `Status` row
117	explicitly does not. The difference is deliberate: ADRs are exempt from the
118	coverage tier, because asking a decision record to cite a test for every
119	statement it makes is the wrong ask of a decision record.
120	
121	`.specify/spec.md` is exempt from this section. It is the repo-level system
122	spec, it predates the convention, and its content is deliberately frozen -
123	giving it a header table and a lead paragraph would mean writing new prose into
124	a file that is meant to stay unchanged. The exemption covers the header table
125	and the lead paragraph only: the Lore coverage job does scan
126	`.specify/spec.md`, so link placement still applies to it.
127	
128	## Spec Test Links
129	
130	Statements in `specs/*/spec.md` cite their validating test in a trailing
131	parenthetical at the end of the statement, where a list item counts as one
132	statement and a paragraph counts per sentence. Tests live beside their source
133	in this repo, so the path points into `src/`:
134	
135	```markdown
136	- All entries within a single assistant response are committed before the next
137	  user message is processed
138	  ([validated by: commits every entry before the next user message](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts#L42)).
139	```
140	
141	The citation carries the test's **name** as well as its line. The name is what the
142	author cited; the line is a derived pointer, and it goes stale on its own - adding
143	an import above a suite moves every test below it, and the citation lands on a
144	different, still-valid declaration without anything noticing. `npm run spec:names`
145	holds each citation to the test it names, and `npm run spec:names:fix` repoints the
146	line from the name. The `#Lnn` stays because the lint rule and the coverage job
147	both index by it; a citation without one marks the whole file covered rather than
148	one test.
149	
150	A citation counts as coverage only where it is trailing, and a test link placed
151	anywhere else in the statement is a misplaced citation rather than a weaker one.
152	Upstream `check:spec-links` reports it and exits 1, and the coverage job that
153	consumes these specs records nothing for it - so a spec can read as fully cited while its coverage is
154	zero. A mid-statement link to something that is not a test file - a script, a
155	doc, another spec - is ordinary prose, is never reported, and was never coverage
156	to begin with. A misplaced citation is fixed by moving it to the end of its
157	statement, never by deleting it.
158	
159	In a test file the `#Lnn` anchor must land on the `it(`, `test(` or `describe(`
160	declaration itself - not a blank line, not one holding only closing punctuation,
161	and not a line inside the test body. A citation onto an `expect` renders and
162	resolves like any other, and proves nothing: no reader can turn that line back
163	into the name of a case. `scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` reports all four as
164	`rotten` and exits 1 in both modes. A citation into a file that is not a test -
165	a workflow, a config, `package.json` - has no declaration to land on and is held
166	only to existing and carrying content.
167	
168	What no gate can catch is an anchor aimed at the wrong declaration: a real but
169	unintended `it(` passes every check. The tell is that the test the statement
170	meant to cite goes on reading as uncited in the `require-spec-link` backlog.
171	
172	Anchors drift silently whenever a cited file gains or loses lines above them, so
173	after editing any cited file re-run `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs`
174	rather than hand-correcting the numbers. That script cannot repair a spec absent
175	from the base ref, since it has no baseline to translate from; on the branch that
176	introduces a spec, its anchors have to be corrected by hand.
177	
178	The convention's tooling is wired up here: `npm run check:spec-links`, `npm run check:spec-status` and
179	`node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs --check origin/main` all gate CI, and
180	`re-lint/require-status-matches-coverage` derives each `Status` row from its
181	spec's citations. `re-lint/require-spec-link` gates in `eslint.config.mjs`: every test cites a
182	statement, so an uncited new test fails the build. Its statement-side mirror,
183	`require-statement-links`, runs at `warn` from `eslint.config.backlog.mjs` and
184	reports without blocking - the severities the rule pair is designed for.
185	
186	## Commit Conventions
187	
188	### Format
189	Follow conventional commits:
190	```
191	<type>(<scope>): <subject>
192	
193	<body>
194	
195	<footer>
196	```
197	
198	### Types
199	- `feat` - New feature (provider, tool, config option)
200	- `fix` - Bug fix
201	- `refactor` - Code restructuring without behavior change
202	- `test` - Test additions or modifications
203	- `docs` - Documentation only
204	- `chore` - Build, deps, config, tooling
205	- `perf` - Performance improvement
206	
207	### Scope
208	Optional but recommended. Use domain areas:
209	- `bedrock` / `vertex` / `openai` / `anthropic` / `mock` - Provider-specific
210	- `tools` - Tool registry and execution
211	- `orchestrator` - Chat orchestrator
212	- `transport` - Express/WebSocket
213	- `session` - Session management
214	- `types` - Type definitions
215	- `build` - Build/packaging
216	
217	### Examples
218	```
219	feat(tools): add parallel tool execution batching
220	fix(bedrock): handle streaming timeouts gracefully
221	refactor(orchestrator): extract context building logic
222	docs(providers): add Vertex AI implementation guide
223	test(tools): add registry conflict detection
224	```
225	
226	### Rules
227	- Use imperative mood: "add" not "added" or "adds"
228	- Do not capitalize first letter of subject
229	- No period (.) at end of subject
230	- Limit subject to 50 characters
231	- Reference issues in footer: `Fixes #123`, `Relates to #456`
232	- Breaking changes in footer: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`
233	
234	## PR Requirements
235	
236	### Before Opening
237	1. Run full check suite and ensure all pass:
238	   ```bash
239	   npm run verify
240	   ```
241	2. Create a feature branch from `main`: `git checkout -b feat/description`
242	3. Commit with conventional format
243	
244	### PR Description Template
245	```markdown
246	## Description
247	Brief summary of changes and rationale.
248	
249	## Type of Change
250	- [ ] Feature
251	- [ ] Bug fix
252	- [ ] Breaking change
253	- [ ] Documentation
254	
255	## Changes
256	- Bullet list of concrete changes
257	- What was added/modified/removed
258	
259	## Testing
260	- How to test locally
261	- Any new test cases added
262	- Edge cases considered
263	
264	## Checklist
265	- [ ] Code follows style guide (eslint passes)
266	- [ ] No console.logs or debugging code
267	- [ ] TypeScript strict mode passes
268	- [ ] Tests added/updated for new behavior
269	- [ ] Documentation updated (README, specs/, adrs/, docs/)
270	- [ ] Spec `Status` rows re-evaluated if any spec gained or lost a test citation
271	- [ ] No new warnings in build output
272	```
273	
274	### Acceptance Criteria
275	- [ ] All GitHub Actions CI checks pass. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is three
276	      jobs - `verify` (sixteen steps, of which `npm run verify` reproduces
277	      fourteen), `build-chain` (audit, action pins) and `smoke` (packed tarball,
278	      both peer variants)
279	- [ ] Reviewed by somebody other than the author. `main` requires a pull request
280	      but is configured for zero required approvals and carries no `CODEOWNERS`,
281	      so this one is convention rather than a gate
282	- [ ] No merge conflicts
283	- [ ] Commit messages follow conventional format
284	- [ ] Tests cover new functionality (aim for >80% coverage on modified files)
285	- [ ] No dependencies added without discussion (especially AI provider SDKs)
286	- [ ] Breaking changes clearly documented and justified
287	- [ ] Public API changes described in `specs/`, not in comments (see Code Style)
288	
289	### Provider Implementation PRs
290	For new provider support:
291	- [ ] Provider in `src/providers/<name>/` with index.ts exporting public API
292	- [ ] Implements `AIProvider` interface fully
293	- [ ] Handles streaming with `MessageChunk` protocol
294	- [ ] Tool/function calling mapped correctly
295	- [ ] Error handling with `AIError` type
296	- [ ] Tests for success and error scenarios
297	- [ ] Added to README.md provider table
298	- [ ] specs/hal-engine-providers/spec.md updated with implementation notes
299	
300	## Compliance Constraints
301	
302	### TypeScript
303	- `strict: true` in tsconfig.json is non-negotiable
304	- All public exports must be typed (no `any` in public APIs)
305	- Use `type` for type-only imports: `import type { ... } from '...'`
306	- Generics preferred over union types for reusability
307	
308	### Code Style
309	- ESLint config: `eslint.config.mjs` (flat config format)
310	- Max warnings: 0 (all warnings treated as errors)
311	- Comments: one line maximum (`re-lint/max-comment-lines`), and it counts a run
312	  of consecutive `//` lines as one comment. JSDoc is **not** exempt — a one-line
313	  `/** … */` passes, a multi-line block does not, which is exactly what
314	  `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` needs. Prose lives in `specs/`, `adrs/` and
315	  `docs/`. Exempt: tooling directives (`eslint-disable`/`eslint-enable`,
316	  `@ts-expect-error`/`@ts-ignore`/`@ts-nocheck`, triple-slash references,
317	  istanbul/c8 hints, `jscpd:ignore`, the shebang). An `eslint-disable` carries
318	  its reason after `--`
319	- Prettier config: `.prettierrc` (run before commit)
320	- Line length: 120 (`printWidth` in `.prettierrc`)
321	- Semicolons: Required
322	- Quotes: Single quotes (`singleQuote: true` in `.prettierrc`)
323	
324	### Testing
325	- Jest configuration: `jest.config.js`
326	- ts-jest for TypeScript support
327	- Minimum coverage: 70% lines for new code. That is review guidance; the gate is
328	  `coverageThreshold` in `jest.config.js`, set to what each path measured rather
329	  than to a flat 70, which had handed four groups an 18-30 point regression budget
330	- The floors ratchet: raise one when coverage rises, never lower one to make a
331	  change pass. A floor that moves down is a regression with the alarm switched off
332	- The exception is a change of instrument. An upgrade that counts branch points the
333	  old version never saw re-reads every floor at once, and a group whose denominator
334	  grew can fall while nothing about the suite changed. Settle it on covered/total
335	  absolutes rather than percentages, and record them where the floors live
336	- All public APIs require at least one test
337	- Async code must have proper await/done handling
338	
339	### Architecture Constraints
340	- **Layered structure mandatory** (types → providers → infrastructure → orchestration → transport)
341	- No circular dependencies between layers
342	- Providers must be pluggable (no hardcoded provider logic in orchestrator)
343	- Session store must be swappable (interface-based)
344	- Tools must be composable and testable in isolation
345	- WebSocket protocol defined in types/messages.ts (additive changes only for backward compatibility)
346	
347	### Dependency Management
348	- Core dependencies only (Express, ws, uuid, cookie, cors, cookie-parser)
349	- `@types/express`, `@types/node` and `@types/ws` are dependencies rather than
350	  devDependencies, because the emitted `.d.ts` files import `express`, `http`,
351	  `stream` and `ws`. Moving them back breaks a consumer's `tsc`, not ours
352	- Provider SDKs as optional peerDependencies
353	- No peer dependency version conflicts
354	- Security: `npm run check:audit` fails at `high` and above on the full installed
355	  tree. Moderate and low advisories do not block. An advisory that cannot be
356	  fixed yet goes in `.github/audit-acknowledgements.json` carrying advisory,
357	  package, reason, ISO expiry and who acknowledged it; an expired entry fails
358	  the gate, so an acceptance cannot become permanent by neglect
359	- License: Apache-2.0, declared in `package.json` and carried in `LICENSE`. No
360	  per-file licence headers: `re-lint/max-comment-lines` caps a comment at one
361	  line and exempts only tooling directives, so the thirteen-line Apache notice
362	  cannot go in a source file. Apache-2.0 recommends headers, it does not
363	  require them
364	
365	### Documentation Requirements
366	- A comment may span at most one line, JSDoc included — see Code Style. What a
367	  public function is and does belongs in `specs/`; what a signature is, the
368	  signature already says
369	- A one-line comment states the one constraint the code cannot show — "why", not
370	  "what". Anything longer goes to `specs/` or `adrs/`
371	- README.md kept in sync with actual features/examples
372	- specs/ directory is source of truth for architecture and protocols; adrs/ records decisions
373	- `.specify/spec.md` is the repo-level system spec. It is ingested by context
374	  tooling and served as authority, so a claim left stale there reaches every
375	  agent that assembles context for this repo. Keep it true when the manifest
376	  changes
377	- `CHANGELOG.md` at the repo root, Keep a Changelog 1.1.0, newest first under
378	  `## [Unreleased]`. Anything a consumer of the published package can observe
379	  gets an entry, written for somebody installing it rather than for somebody
380	  reading this repo's commit log. Enforced in CI: a pull request touching
381	  non-test files under `src/` fails unless it also touches `CHANGELOG.md`, and
382	  the `no-changelog` label is the deliberate escape hatch for a change nothing
383	  installable observes. Not derived from commit messages - a release note and a
384	  commit subject have different readers
385	
386	### Releasing
387	- Five human steps: bump `version` in `package.json` inside the pull request,
388	  merge it, draft a GitHub Release on `main` tagged `vX.Y.Z`, publish it, approve
389	  the staged version. Everything between the release and the approval is CI
390	- Release notes are hand-written on Keep a Changelog 1.1.0, not generated from
391	  commit subjects. The audience is somebody installing the package, who cannot
392	  act on `refactor(transport):` and needs to know what changed for them
393	- Rename `CHANGELOG.md`'s `## [Unreleased]` heading to the version being
394	  released in that same pull request, and open a fresh `## [Unreleased]` above it.
395	  `npm run check:version -- vX.Y.Z` fails if the heading does not name the version
396	- Run `npm run check:version -- vX.Y.Z` before publishing the release. A release
397	  and its tag can be deleted; an approved version cannot be replaced, and after
398	  72 hours cannot be withdrawn
399	- The tag must be `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` and match `package.json` exactly.
400	  Prerelease tags are rejected because nothing passes `--tag`, so one would
401	  publish as `latest` and every plain `npm install` would resolve to it. A
402	  release ticked as a pre-release is refused before a runner starts
403	- Cut the release from a commit already merged to `main`. The workflow refuses a
404	  tag whose commit is not an ancestor of `origin/main`: a release can be drafted
405	  against any branch or commit, so without that check the protection on `main` is
406	  not the boundary the release rests on
407	- `.github/workflows/publish.yml` runs on a published release. A draft fires
408	  nothing, and `workflow_dispatch` on the release's tag is how a publish that
409	  failed after the release exists is re-run. It re-runs the version guard, the
410	  build-chain checks and the packed-tarball smoke test against the tagged commit,
411	  and refuses a pack list carrying any `*.test.*` entry, before anything is
412	  published. A tag points wherever its author chose, so a green run on `main` is
413	  not evidence about what is being released
414	- Authentication is npm Trusted Publishing over OIDC. There is no `NPM_TOKEN`
415	  secret, and the trusted publisher is registered against the workflow file's
416	  path - renaming or moving `publish.yml` stops publishing until it is
417	  re-registered
418	- The publish carries `--provenance`, which is available only because ADR-007
419	  makes the source repository public
420	- The publish is staged. The workflow puts the tarball, its dist-tag and its
421	  provenance on the registry, and the version stays uninstallable until a
422	  maintainer approves it with 2FA - the package page's Versions tab, or
423	  `npm stage list` then `npm stage approve <id>`. A staged version nobody
424	  approves reaches nobody, which is the closest thing to an undo that exists
425	  once a tag has fired
426	
427	### Breaking Changes
428	- MUST be discussed in issue before implementation
429	- MUST include migration guide in PR
430	- MUST increment MINOR version (semver)
431	- MUST update README quick start example if API changes
432	- MUST publish the migration guide as a `### Changed` entry in `CHANGELOG.md` as
433	  well as in the pull request: the PR is where reviewers read it, the changelog is
434	  where the consumer it affects reads it
435	- MUST add deprecation period (1 minor version) when possible. The unit is a
436	  published registry version and the audience is a consumer resolving one:
437	  a deprecation runs from the version that announces it to the version that
438	  removes the behaviour. A consumer on a git specifier is outside the clause -
439	  they pin a commit, so nothing announces anything to them and no minor
440	  elapses on their side
441	
442	### AI Provider Compliance
443	- No hardcoded API keys or secrets (use environment variables)
444	- Providers must handle rate limiting gracefully
445	- Tool calling must match JSON Schema spec
446	- Streaming must support cancellation/cleanup
447	- Usage tracking must be optional (SessionStore integration)
448	- Error messages must be actionable (not raw SDK errors)

14. **.specify/spec.md** - Repo-level system spec (exempt from the spec header table convention)

## Workflow Commands

### Development
```bash
npm run dev          # Start example/server.ts with hot reload (tsx watch)
npm run typecheck    # Run TypeScript type checking without emitting
```

### Building
```bash
npm run build        # Compile TypeScript to dist/ (tsc)
npm start            # Run compiled JavaScript from dist/index.js
```

### Testing
```bash
npm test             # Run Jest test suite
# Tests use ts-jest for TypeScript compilation
# Configuration: jest.config.js
```

### Code Quality
```bash
npm run eslint       # Run ESLint with max-warnings 0 (zero-tolerance)
npm run prettier     # Format all src/**/*.ts with Prettier
npm run prettier:check  # Check formatting without writing
```

### All Checks (Recommended Pre-Commit)
```bash
npm run verify
```

That is the blocking set `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `verify` job runs on every
pull request, in the same order, and `scripts/verify-script.test.ts` fails if the
two stop agreeing - so this command cannot quietly become a subset of what CI
demands. Two gates in that job are missing from it because both diff against
`origin/main` and neither runs the same way on a checkout: the spec anchor check
and the changelog check.

Two further CI jobs are worth running locally before a release or a change that
touches packaging: `npm run check:build-chain` (audit and action pins) and
`npm run smoke` (packs the tarball and installs it outside this tree).

## Spec Header Table

Every `specs/*/spec.md` opens with its title, then a two-column header table,
and carries a lead paragraph of prose before its first `##` section:

```markdown
# <spec title>

| Field  | Value                  |
| ------ | ---------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#<n> |
| Status | Draft                  |

<lead paragraph>
```

The lead paragraph does not have to sit immediately after the table: a spec
carrying a metadata block of its own may place that block between the two. What
the convention requires is that prose, rather than a section heading, follows
the header material, and that the prose runs to at least 40 characters -
anything shorter is reported as no lead paragraph at all.

`Issue` names the issue the spec was written against, or `n/a` for the specs
that predate this convention.

`Status` is one of `Draft`, `In Progress` or `Shipped`. It is not a mood, and
it is not a claim about how finished the feature is: it is the spec's own
test-citation coverage. No testable statement cited is `Draft`, some cited is
`In Progress`, all cited is `Shipped`. A spec describing shipped, working
behaviour still reads `Draft` until its statements cite the tests that
validate them.

A spec that should no longer be graded takes a terminal value instead. The
parser buckets roughly sixteen labels into five buckets, and the two terminal
ones skip the coverage check whatever the citation count:

| Written into the spec                                            | Bucket                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `Draft`                                                          | `draft`                      |
| `In Progress`, `In Review`, `Planning`, `WIP`, `Proposed`        | `in-progress`                |
| `Shipped`, `Implemented`, `Complete`, `Accepted`, `Done`, `Live` | `shipped`                    |
| `Retired`, `Superseded`, `Removed`, `Deprecated`, `Obsolete`     | `retired` - skips the check  |
| `Rejected`, `Abandoned`                                          | `rejected` - skips the check |

Prefer the canonical `Draft` / `In Progress` / `Shipped` for a live spec; reach
for `Retired` or `Rejected` rather than leaving a superseded spec to claim a
coverage tier it will never earn.

ADRs do not carry this table. They declare their state as YAML frontmatter
`status:` instead - `accepted` for a decision the code implements, `proposed`
for one it does not. That field does mean maturity, which the spec `Status` row
explicitly does not. The difference is deliberate: ADRs are exempt from the
coverage tier, because asking a decision record to cite a test for every
statement it makes is the wrong ask of a decision record.

`.specify/spec.md` is exempt from this section. It is the repo-level system
spec, it predates the convention, and its content is deliberately frozen -
giving it a header table and a lead paragraph would mean writing new prose into
a file that is meant to stay unchanged. The exemption covers the header table
and the lead paragraph only: the Lore coverage job does scan
`.specify/spec.md`, so link placement still applies to it.

## Spec Test Links

Statements in `specs/*/spec.md` cite their validating test in a trailing
parenthetical at the end of the statement, where a list item counts as one
statement and a paragraph counts per sentence. Tests live beside their source
in this repo, so the path points into `src/`:

```markdown
- All entries within a single assistant response are committed before the next
  user message is processed
  ([validated by: commits every entry before the next user message](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts#L42)).
```

The citation carries the test's **name** as well as its line. The name is what the
author cited; the line is a derived pointer, and it goes stale on its own - adding
an import above a suite moves every test below it, and the citation lands on a
different, still-valid declaration without anything noticing. `npm run spec:names`
holds each citation to the test it names, and `npm run spec:names:fix` repoints the
line from the name. The `#Lnn` stays because the lint rule and the coverage job
both index by it; a citation without one marks the whole file covered rather than
one test.

A citation counts as coverage only where it is trailing, and a test link placed
anywhere else in the statement is a misplaced citation rather than a weaker one.
Upstream `check:spec-links` reports it and exits 1, and the coverage job that
consumes these specs records nothing for it - so a spec can read as fully cited while its coverage is
zero. A mid-statement link to something that is not a test file - a script, a
doc, another spec - is ordinary prose, is never reported, and was never coverage
to begin with. A misplaced citation is fixed by moving it to the end of its
statement, never by deleting it.

In a test file the `#Lnn` anchor must land on the `it(`, `test(` or `describe(`
declaration itself - not a blank line, not one holding only closing punctuation,
and not a line inside the test body. A citation onto an `expect` renders and
resolves like any other, and proves nothing: no reader can turn that line back
into the name of a case. `scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` reports all four as
`rotten` and exits 1 in both modes. A citation into a file that is not a test -
a workflow, a config, `package.json` - has no declaration to land on and is held
only to existing and carrying content.

What no gate can catch is an anchor aimed at the wrong declaration: a real but
unintended `it(` passes every check. The tell is that the test the statement
meant to cite goes on reading as uncited in the `require-spec-link` backlog.

Anchors drift silently whenever a cited file gains or loses lines above them, so
after editing any cited file re-run `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs`
rather than hand-correcting the numbers. That script cannot repair a spec absent
from the base ref, since it has no baseline to translate from; on the branch that
introduces a spec, its anchors have to be corrected by hand.

The convention's tooling is wired up here: `npm run check:spec-links`, `npm run check:spec-status` and
`node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs --check origin/main` all gate CI, and
`re-lint/require-status-matches-coverage` derives each `Status` row from its
spec's citations. `re-lint/require-spec-link` gates in `eslint.config.mjs`: every test cites a
statement, so an uncited new test fails the build. Its statement-side mirror,
`require-statement-links`, runs at `warn` from `eslint.config.backlog.mjs` and
reports without blocking - the severities the rule pair is designed for.

## Commit Conventions

### Format
Follow conventional commits:
```
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

<body>

<footer>
```

### Types
- `feat` - New feature (provider, tool, config option)
- `fix` - Bug fix
- `refactor` - Code restructuring without behavior change
- `test` - Test additions or modifications
- `docs` - Documentation only
- `chore` - Build, deps, config, tooling
- `perf` - Performance improvement

### Scope
Optional but recommended. Use domain areas:
- `bedrock` / `vertex` / `openai` / `anthropic` / `mock` - Provider-specific
- `tools` - Tool registry and execution
- `orchestrator` - Chat orchestrator
- `transport` - Express/WebSocket
- `session` - Session management
- `types` - Type definitions
- `build` - Build/packaging

### Examples
```
feat(tools): add parallel tool execution batching
fix(bedrock): handle streaming timeouts gracefully
refactor(orchestrator): extract context building logic
docs(providers): add Vertex AI implementation guide
test(tools): add registry conflict detection
```

### Rules
- Use imperative mood: "add" not "added" or "adds"
- Do not capitalize first letter of subject
- No period (.) at end of subject
- Limit subject to 50 characters
- Reference issues in footer: `Fixes #123`, `Relates to #456`
- Breaking changes in footer: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`

## PR Requirements

### Before Opening
1. Run full check suite and ensure all pass:
   ```bash
   npm run verify
   ```
2. Create a feature branch from `main`: `git checkout -b feat/description`
3. Commit with conventional format

### PR Description Template
```markdown
## Description
Brief summary of changes and rationale.

## Type of Change
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation

## Changes
- Bullet list of concrete changes
- What was added/modified/removed

## Testing
- How to test locally
- Any new test cases added
- Edge cases considered

## Checklist
- [ ] Code follows style guide (eslint passes)
- [ ] No console.logs or debugging code
- [ ] TypeScript strict mode passes
- [ ] Tests added/updated for new behavior
- [ ] Documentation updated (README, specs/, adrs/, docs/)
- [ ] Spec `Status` rows re-evaluated if any spec gained or lost a test citation
- [ ] No new warnings in build output
```

### Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All GitHub Actions CI checks pass. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is three
      jobs - `verify` (sixteen steps, of which `npm run verify` reproduces
      fourteen), `build-chain` (audit, action pins) and `smoke` (packed tarball,
      both peer variants)
- [ ] Reviewed by somebody other than the author. `main` requires a pull request
      but is configured for zero required approvals and carries no `CODEOWNERS`,
      so this one is convention rather than a gate
- [ ] No merge conflicts
- [ ] Commit messages follow conventional format
- [ ] Tests cover new functionality (aim for >80% coverage on modified files)
- [ ] No dependencies added without discussion (especially AI provider SDKs)
- [ ] Breaking changes clearly documented and justified
- [ ] Public API changes described in `specs/`, not in comments (see Code Style)

### Provider Implementation PRs
For new provider support:
- [ ] Provider in `src/providers/<name>/` with index.ts exporting public API
- [ ] Implements `AIProvider` interface fully
- [ ] Handles streaming with `MessageChunk` protocol
- [ ] Tool/function calling mapped correctly
- [ ] Error handling with `AIError` type
- [ ] Tests for success and error scenarios
- [ ] Added to README.md provider table
- [ ] specs/hal-engine-providers/spec.md updated with implementation notes

## Compliance Constraints

### TypeScript
- `strict: true` in tsconfig.json is non-negotiable
- All public exports must be typed (no `any` in public APIs)
- Use `type` for type-only imports: `import type { ... } from '...'`
- Generics preferred over union types for reusability

### Code Style
- ESLint config: `eslint.config.mjs` (flat config format)
- Max warnings: 0 (all warnings treated as errors)
- Comments: one line maximum (`re-lint/max-comment-lines`), and it counts a run
  of consecutive `//` lines as one comment. JSDoc is **not** exempt — a one-line
  `/** … */` passes, a multi-line block does not, which is exactly what
  `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` needs. Prose lives in `specs/`, `adrs/` and
  `docs/`. Exempt: tooling directives (`eslint-disable`/`eslint-enable`,
  `@ts-expect-error`/`@ts-ignore`/`@ts-nocheck`, triple-slash references,
  istanbul/c8 hints, `jscpd:ignore`, the shebang). An `eslint-disable` carries
  its reason after `--`
- Prettier config: `.prettierrc` (run before commit)
- Line length: 120 (`printWidth` in `.prettierrc`)
- Semicolons: Required
- Quotes: Single quotes (`singleQuote: true` in `.prettierrc`)

### Testing
- Jest configuration: `jest.config.js`
- ts-jest for TypeScript support
- Minimum coverage: 70% lines for new code. That is review guidance; the gate is
  `coverageThreshold` in `jest.config.js`, set to what each path measured rather
  than to a flat 70, which had handed four groups an 18-30 point regression budget
- The floors ratchet: raise one when coverage rises, never lower one to make a
  change pass. A floor that moves down is a regression with the alarm switched off
- The exception is a change of instrument. An upgrade that counts branch points the
  old version never saw re-reads every floor at once, and a group whose denominator
  grew can fall while nothing about the suite changed. Settle it on covered/total
  absolutes rather than percentages, and record them where the floors live
- All public APIs require at least one test
- Async code must have proper await/done handling

### Architecture Constraints
- **Layered structure mandatory** (types → providers → infrastructure → orchestration → transport)
- No circular dependencies between layers
- Providers must be pluggable (no hardcoded provider logic in orchestrator)
- Session store must be swappable (interface-based)
- Tools must be composable and testable in isolation
- WebSocket protocol defined in types/messages.ts (additive changes only for backward compatibility)

### Dependency Management
- Core dependencies only (Express, ws, uuid, cookie, cors, cookie-parser)
- `@types/express`, `@types/node` and `@types/ws` are dependencies rather than
  devDependencies, because the emitted `.d.ts` files import `express`, `http`,
  `stream` and `ws`. Moving them back breaks a consumer's `tsc`, not ours
- Provider SDKs as optional peerDependencies
- No peer dependency version conflicts
- Security: `npm run check:audit` fails at `high` and above on the full installed
  tree. Moderate and low advisories do not block. An advisory that cannot be
  fixed yet goes in `.github/audit-acknowledgements.json` carrying advisory,
  package, reason, ISO expiry and who acknowledged it; an expired entry fails
  the gate, so an acceptance cannot become permanent by neglect
- License: Apache-2.0, declared in `package.json` and carried in `LICENSE`. No
  per-file licence headers: `re-lint/max-comment-lines` caps a comment at one
  line and exempts only tooling directives, so the thirteen-line Apache notice
  cannot go in a source file. Apache-2.0 recommends headers, it does not
  require them

### Documentation Requirements
- A comment may span at most one line, JSDoc included — see Code Style. What a
  public function is and does belongs in `specs/`; what a signature is, the
  signature already says
- A one-line comment states the one constraint the code cannot show — "why", not
  "what". Anything longer goes to `specs/` or `adrs/`
- README.md kept in sync with actual features/examples
- specs/ directory is source of truth for architecture and protocols; adrs/ records decisions
- `.specify/spec.md` is the repo-level system spec. It is ingested by context
  tooling and served as authority, so a claim left stale there reaches every
  agent that assembles context for this repo. Keep it true when the manifest
  changes
- `CHANGELOG.md` at the repo root, Keep a Changelog 1.1.0, newest first under
  `## [Unreleased]`. Anything a consumer of the published package can observe
  gets an entry, written for somebody installing it rather than for somebody
  reading this repo's commit log. Enforced in CI: a pull request touching
  non-test files under `src/` fails unless it also touches `CHANGELOG.md`, and
  the `no-changelog` label is the deliberate escape hatch for a change nothing
  installable observes. Not derived from commit messages - a release note and a
  commit subject have different readers

### Releasing
- Five human steps: bump `version` in `package.json` inside the pull request,
  merge it, draft a GitHub Release on `main` tagged `vX.Y.Z`, publish it, approve
  the staged version. Everything between the release and the approval is CI
- Release notes are hand-written on Keep a Changelog 1.1.0, not generated from
  commit subjects. The audience is somebody installing the package, who cannot
  act on `refactor(transport):` and needs to know what changed for them
- Rename `CHANGELOG.md`'s `## [Unreleased]` heading to the version being
  released in that same pull request, and open a fresh `## [Unreleased]` above it.
  `npm run check:version -- vX.Y.Z` fails if the heading does not name the version
- Run `npm run check:version -- vX.Y.Z` before publishing the release. A release
  and its tag can be deleted; an approved version cannot be replaced, and after
  72 hours cannot be withdrawn
- The tag must be `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` and match `package.json` exactly.
  Prerelease tags are rejected because nothing passes `--tag`, so one would
  publish as `latest` and every plain `npm install` would resolve to it. A
  release ticked as a pre-release is refused before a runner starts
- Cut the release from a commit already merged to `main`. The workflow refuses a
  tag whose commit is not an ancestor of `origin/main`: a release can be drafted
  against any branch or commit, so without that check the protection on `main` is
  not the boundary the release rests on
- `.github/workflows/publish.yml` runs on a published release. A draft fires
  nothing, and `workflow_dispatch` on the release's tag is how a publish that
  failed after the release exists is re-run. It re-runs the version guard, the
  build-chain checks and the packed-tarball smoke test against the tagged commit,
  and refuses a pack list carrying any `*.test.*` entry, before anything is
  published. A tag points wherever its author chose, so a green run on `main` is
  not evidence about what is being released
- Authentication is npm Trusted Publishing over OIDC. There is no `NPM_TOKEN`
  secret, and the trusted publisher is registered against the workflow file's
  path - renaming or moving `publish.yml` stops publishing until it is
  re-registered
- The publish carries `--provenance`, which is available only because ADR-007
  makes the source repository public
- The publish is staged. The workflow puts the tarball, its dist-tag and its
  provenance on the registry, and the version stays uninstallable until a
  maintainer approves it with 2FA - the package page's Versions tab, or
  `npm stage list` then `npm stage approve <id>`. A staged version nobody
  approves reaches nobody, which is the closest thing to an undo that exists
  once a tag has fired

### Breaking Changes
- MUST be discussed in issue before implementation
- MUST include migration guide in PR
- MUST increment MINOR version (semver)
- MUST update README quick start example if API changes
- MUST publish the migration guide as a `### Changed` entry in `CHANGELOG.md` as
  well as in the pull request: the PR is where reviewers read it, the changelog is
  where the consumer it affects reads it
- MUST add deprecation period (1 minor version) when possible. The unit is a
  published registry version and the audience is a consumer resolving one:
  a deprecation runs from the version that announces it to the version that
  removes the behaviour. A consumer on a git specifier is outside the clause -
  they pin a commit, so nothing announces anything to them and no minor
  elapses on their side

### AI Provider Compliance
- No hardcoded API keys or secrets (use environment variables)
- Providers must handle rate limiting gracefully
- Tool calling must match JSON Schema spec
- Streaming must support cancellation/cleanup
- Usage tracking must be optional (SessionStore integration)
- Error messages must be actionable (not raw SDK errors)

# @re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint

re:cinq's house ESLint rules for TypeScript repositories: complexity budgets,
naming, function shape, comments, tests, folder layering, spec traceability,
and jscpd-backed duplicate detection. Flat config only. The plugin key is
`re-lint`, so every rule reads `re-lint/<name>`.

The rules were extracted from the [re-cinq/lore](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore)
monorepo, where each one was introduced against a real failure mode and driven
to zero findings before being promoted to `error`. Most of them encode the
Clean Code cheat-sheet; the mapping is at the end of this document.

## Install

```sh
npm i -D @re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint eslint typescript-eslint
```

Optional peers, needed only by the rules that use them:

| Peer                       | Needed by                                                                                           |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@stylistic/eslint-plugin` | the `recommended` preset's blank-line rules (pass it in; omitted otherwise)                         |
| `@eslint/markdown`         | the four markdown rules (`require-*`, `no-dead-md-links`), which run under `language: markdown/gfm` |
| `typescript`               | `no-forwarding-class` (type-aware; needs `parserOptions.projectService`)                            |
| `jscpd` (5.x)              | `no-duplicate-code`                                                                                 |

Node 20 or newer, ESLint 9 or newer.

## Quick start

The `recommended` preset switches on every rule that needs no repository
knowledge, plus the ESLint core and typescript-eslint rules that back the
same guidelines (`complexity` 6, `max-lines-per-function` 30, `max-params` 3,
`max-depth` 2, `no-magic-numbers`, `id-length`, `no-negated-condition`,
`naming-convention` without `I` prefixes or `Type` suffixes, and more).
`typescript-eslint` and `@stylistic/eslint-plugin` are passed in rather than
imported, so the package depends on neither; leave one out and its rules are
left out too.

```js
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";
import stylistic from "@stylistic/eslint-plugin";
import reLint from "@re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint";

export default tseslint.config(
  { ignores: ["dist/**", "node_modules/**"] },
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  ...reLint.configs.recommended({ tseslint, stylistic }),
);
```

Or wire rules by hand:

```js
import reLint from "@re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint";

export default [
  {
    files: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"],
    plugins: { "re-lint": reLint },
    rules: {
      "re-lint/no-nested-if": "error",
      "re-lint/no-flag-params": "error",
      "re-lint/max-boolean-operators": ["error", { max: 2 }],
    },
  },
];
```

Every rule is `error` in the preset. Repositories adopting the package on an
existing codebase override the noisy ones to `warn` (see
[Adopting in an existing repository](#adopting-in-an-existing-repository)).

## Rule reference

Options are listed with their defaults. "Preset" says whether the rule is in
`configs.recommended`; rules marked "opt-in" need an option or a `files` scope
that only the consumer knows, and report nothing until they get it.

### Complexity and control flow

| Rule                       | Reports                                                                                                                                 | Options                                                      | Fix | Preset |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ------ |
| `no-nested-if`             | an `if` inside another `if` in the same function; `else if` chains are one level                                                        |                                                              |     | yes    |
| `no-nested-loop`           | a loop inside another loop in the same function                                                                                         |                                                              |     | yes    |
| `prefer-early-return`      | a function whose body is one big `if`; inverts it into a guard clause                                                                   |                                                              | yes | yes    |
| `max-boolean-operators`    | a condition or assignment with more than `max` `&&`/`\|\|` operators; extract a named predicate                                         | `max: 2`                                                     |     | yes    |
| `no-catch-as-control-flow` | a `catch` that swallows or branches on an error instead of handling it                                                                  |                                                              |     | yes    |
| `prefer-polymorphism`      | a `switch` or if/else-if chain dispatching on an object's tag (`x.type`, `x.kind`) with `minCases` or more branches                     | `minCases: 3`, `discriminants: []` (any property when empty) |     | yes    |
| `max-member-chain`         | a member chain deeper than `max` hops (Law of Demeter); `this`, well-known globals, `allowRoots`, and all-call fluent chains are exempt | `max: 2`, `allowRoots: []`                                   |     | yes    |

### Names

| Rule                              | Reports                                                                                                             | Options                                    | Fix | Preset                        |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | --- | ----------------------------- |
| `no-vague-names`                  | declarations named `data`, `temp`, `obj`, `x`, and the rest of the blocklist                                        | `names: [...]` (replaces the default list) |     | yes                           |
| `no-negative-names`               | `isNotReady`, `notFound`, `hasNoItems`, `disableX`, `hideX`, `preventX`; suggests the positive name                 | `allow: []`                                |     | yes                           |
| `default-export-matches-filename` | a default export whose name differs from the file's; for Next.js app dirs, `reserved` files must be pure re-exports | `reserved: "error" \| "off"`               |     | opt-in (scope to the app dir) |

```sh
npm i -D @re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint eslint typescript-eslint
```

Optional peers, needed only by the rules that use them:

| Peer                       | Needed by                                                                                           |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@stylistic/eslint-plugin` | the `recommended` preset's blank-line rules (pass it in; omitted otherwise)                         |
| `@eslint/markdown`         | the four markdown rules (`require-*`, `no-dead-md-links`), which run under `language: markdown/gfm` |
| `typescript`               | `no-forwarding-class` (type-aware; needs `parserOptions.projectService`)                            |
| `jscpd` (5.x)              | `no-duplicate-code`                                                                                 |

Node 20 or newer, ESLint 9 or newer.

## Quick start

The `recommended` preset switches on every rule that needs no repository
knowledge, plus the ESLint core and typescript-eslint rules that back the
same guidelines (`complexity` 6, `max-lines-per-function` 30, `max-params` 3,
`max-depth` 2, `no-magic-numbers`, `id-length`, `no-negated-condition`,
`naming-convention` without `I` prefixes or `Type` suffixes, and more).
`typescript-eslint` and `@stylistic/eslint-plugin` are passed in rather than
imported, so the package depends on neither; leave one out and its rules are
left out too.

```js
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";
import stylistic from "@stylistic/eslint-plugin";
import reLint from "@re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint";

export default tseslint.config(
  { ignores: ["dist/**", "node_modules/**"] },
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  ...reLint.configs.recommended({ tseslint, stylistic }),
);
```

Or wire rules by hand:

```js
import reLint from "@re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint";

export default [
  {
    files: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"],
    plugins: { "re-lint": reLint },
    rules: {
      "re-lint/no-nested-if": "error",
      "re-lint/no-flag-params": "error",
      "re-lint/max-boolean-operators": ["error", { max: 2 }],
    },
  },
];
```

Every rule is `error` in the preset. Repositories adopting the package on an
existing codebase override the noisy ones to `warn` (see
[Adopting in an existing repository](#adopting-in-an-existing-repository)).

# Tool Input Validation

| Field  | Value                |
| ------ | -------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |
| Status | In Progress          |

Every tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.

## Validation at execute time
